quotes.text: An operation can report late and still not threaten the due date if there's time later in the route.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Distinguishes a late operation from one that actually controls delivery.

quotes.text: The route tells you where the part should go, it doesn't tell you when the part can actually go there.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Explains in one sentence why a routing is not a critical path.

quotes.text: Touchtime tells you how long someone works on the part. Flowtime tells you how long the customer waits. Those are different measures.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: A memorable contrast between processing time and the waiting the customer experiences.

quotes.text: It comes from treating quality as separate from flow. Quality is part of flow. It decides whether the product can proceed.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Frames quality holds as part of the production path rather than an afterthought.

quotes.text: So prediction tells you what may happen, scheduling tells you what can happen, and optimization helps choose among the schedules that can happen based on goals somebody has explicitly said.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Clearly separates three planning disciplines that are often confused.

takeaways: In production the critical path is the chain of remaining dependencies that controls the earliest completion date right now, and it moves when machines, material, people or quality conditions change.

A routing, a status dashboard or a Power BI report shows intent and symptoms, but a live dependency model with explicit links between orders, operations, resources and release conditions is needed to explain why a date moved.
Prediction, scheduling and optimization answer different questions, and generative AI should explain schedule results rather than invent the schedule itself.
hook: A planned completion date looks reasonable until one operation runs late, a material release slips or a resource disappears, and every downstream promise moves with it. This episode shows manufacturing planners and IT/OT architects how to apply critical path thinking to live production, from shared machines and quality holds to MES, ERP, Microsoft Fabric and knowledge graphs, so they can see which dependency controls delivery now.
